John Marshall. Born in seventeen fifty-five and died in eighteen thirty-five, he was the fourth Chief Justice of the United States and the most influential jurist in American history. His interpretation of the Constitution established judicial review, expanded federal power, and shaped American constitutional law for two centuries. His landmark decisions transformed the Supreme Court from a minor institution into a co-equal branch of government capable of striking down legislative and executive acts.

Marshall was born in Virginia and served as a soldier in the Continental Army, later practicing law. He was appointed to Congress, served briefly as Secretary of State under John Adams, and then appointed Chief Justice in eighteen hundred and one, a position he held for thirty-four years until his death. His most consequential decision was Marbury v. Madison in eighteen hundred and three, where the Court invalidated a minor provision of the Judiciary Act of seventeen eighty-nine, establishing the principle of judicial review, the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional and void.

His expansive interpretation of federal power in McCulloch v. Maryland in eighteen nineteen upheld the constitutionality of the Bank of the United States and asserted that the Constitution's necessary and proper clause gave Congress broad powers. He rejected state claims to nullify federal law. Gibbons v. Ogden in eighteen twenty-four established a broad interpretation of Congress's commerce clause authority, empowering the federal government to regulate interstate commerce and preempt state regulations. This decision undergirded federal regulatory power for centuries.

Marshall's jurisprudence consistently favored national over state power, contractual property rights over populist claims, and judicial authority over executive and legislative prerogatives. These principles aligned with Federalist ideology and influenced American constitutional development. His long tenure from eighteen hundred and one to eighteen thirty-five allowed him to shape the Court during crucial decades. His consensus-building and moderate tone, despite bold constitutional innovations, gave his decisions credibility and durability. He shares connections with the United States Constitution, the document he interpreted to establish judicial power, with the Supreme Court, the Court he transformed from minor to co-equal branch, and with Marbury v. Madison, his most famous decision establishing judicial review.
